goal_title: Book: Graph Theory: What Connections Permit — improvements from the spine reading
why: The whole spine was read as a book on 2026-09-24, one sequence at a time, and every stumble, false claim or broken handover in graphtheory became a task Palle can pick up one at a time. Reader: the VR visitor.
success_criteria: every open task here is done or skipped with a note
the chapters read through without a stumble in the headset
every code excerpt and number in the chapters matches the source

book.title: Graph Theory: What Connections Permit
chapters_read: ML_Synthesis (last of machinelearning, for the handover in)
Euclid_Parallel (first of foundationscrisis, for the handover out)

reading.arc: Eight halls ask one question each of the same kind of object, a set of vertices and permitted connections, and each hall changes the question rather than the object. It opens by separating the graph from the order in which it is visited (two travellers on one tree), then from the positions used to draw it (a spring layout), then shows a route re-found when a connection is withdrawn (a stone sinks). The middle halls turn to what can be measured and claimed: drawn prominence against counted degree, directed reachability and the return path, the cheapest connecting skeleton against each traveller's own trip. The last two halls carry the sequence's real argument: a locally valid step (a forward push, a greedy pair) can close off a better arrangement, and only a procedure that can undo its own choices recovers it. The whole runs on the sequence truth (the same connections host different journeys; what the representation leaves out cannot be recovered by rerouting) and hands Foundations Crisis the distinction that a rule met is not a conclusion proved.
holds: The 'keep it in view' refrain: every hall opens with a short instruction to choose one element (a lamp, a vertex, a stone, an outer point) and hold it while the procedure runs, and the chapter then reads the procedure from that element's side rather than from the animation's confidence.

The carried object is the traveller's memory. The queue and stack of Foundations are picked up by name in Connectivity ('The stack you met with the two travellers now carries information about a question that remains open during the walk'), and the waiting branch of Foundations returns as the unmatched vertex of Matching.

Revision as the through-line of the second half: Pathfinding's replanning, Flow's missing reverse residual ('could some of what was sent earlier be taken back?'), Matching's 'Improving the first result requires undoing an accepted edge'. The exit lines chain it: 'Once again, an early acceptable choice may need to be undone.'

Representation before value: each hall ends by refusing to let its measure stand for worth. Waiting time behind a neat animation, 'an unsupported story about influence', ''Minimum' refers to that sum, not to every traveller's individual journey', 'Maximising a count cannot establish consent, suitability or fairness'.

One shape for eight chapters: a title, a one-line question, one anchored work, six or seven paragraphs at about 400 words, an exit line naming the next hall's question. The sameness is what makes the sequence feel like one voice; at length it is also a stumble (see the backlog paragraphs).

hall_notes.note: Breadth-first and depth-first on a fifteen-lamp tree that alternates by itself; the chapter moves from watching to naming (queue, stack) and closes on waiting time as the ordering rule's consequence. Reads cleanly, but the hall's own readout names the two travellers THE TIDE and THE DIVER and the chapter never does.

The connection-versus-coordinate distinction on an eight-vertex cube drawn by springs and repulsion; the exercise of naming an endpoint by its neighbours instead of by left/right is the sequence's best small task. 'Its positions are adjustable' invites a grab nothing answers, and the drawing settles once with no way to re-tangle it.

A spark commutes across stepping stones on the engine's AStar3D; a push button sinks a stone on its route, three at most, the oldest resurfacing. The chapter's care about 'the graph the search can use' is exact; it trips by asking the reader to watch a displayed, highlighted, bright route that is only ever the spark's walk.

The one chapter that says openly the room cannot yet do what its title asks, and turns that into a method: count degree yourself against a display whose centralities are assigned. Honest and useful, but its first instruction sends the visitor to 'displayed network measures' that are two inert ball-on-bar meters with no number on them.

Strongly connected components by Tarjan's single pass; the advice to test a proposed component from more than one start and the 'one additional return connection' observation are strong teaching. It relies on watching the moment components are discharged together, and the run happens once, seconds after the hall builds, with no in-world restart.

Kruskal on a ten-vertex euclidean graph, accept/reject read as a cycle check; the shift from 'cheap connection' to 'surviving a failure' is the sequence's clearest turn of question. The watch-the-next-edge exercise is undercut by the code: considered edges turn yellow and stay yellow whether they were accepted or rejected.

Forward-only push/relabel with capacity, flow, excess and height as four named quantities, and the BLOCKED end state made into the lesson rather than hidden. The most carefully revised chapter; the negative excess printed on the source sphere is the one readout its definitions do not cover.

The payoff: a five-cycle with five spokes, ORDER/STEP/RUN/RESET push buttons, three pairs versus five from the same connections, and every number checks against the scan order in the code. The longest and the best chapter; one sentence about the source file name is a developer's aside inside a visitor's room.

stumbles: GT_Pathfinding: 'Watch the displayed route change', 'the newly highlighted one', 'a bright route is the spark's calculated route'. No route is drawn; there is the spark's hop-by-hop walk and a readout saying 'route: N stones'. The reader looks for a line and finds none.

GT_Network_Analysis: 'Then look at the displayed network measures. Ask which of those quantities you could independently check'. The scene's two meters never move and carry no number, and 'an animated number appears authoritative' describes nothing in the hall.
GT_Layout: 'Its positions are adjustable'. A headset visitor reaches for a vertex; the artifact takes no input at all.

GT_Layout: 'Keep those relationships in view while the drawing settles'. The layout settles once from the frame the hall builds, and a visitor walking the seven cells from the spawn may meet a drawing that has finished moving, with nothing to restart it.

GT_Connectivity, GT_Spanning_Trees, GT_Flow: 'Watch the moment several vertices receive one component colour', 'Watch the next edge considered by the display', 'Watch for a PUSH or RELABEL step' each describe a one-shot run whose only restart is a keyboard action. Matching's button panel is the model the other three lack.

GT_Spanning_Trees: a rejected edge is never marked and the current-edge yellow is never cleared, so after the first rejection 'the next edge considered' is one yellow line among several, and the green tree is drawn as a second line over yellow at the same coordinates.
GT_Foundations: 'One traveller... The other...' while the readout beside the lamps alternates THE TIDE - BFS and THE DIVER - DFS; the reader has to make the match unaided.
GT_Flow: the green source sphere reads a negative e: value while the chapter defines excess as 'more has arrived than has yet left'.
GT_Matching: 'The artifact retains the source name `edmonds_algorithm`'. The visitor sees GREEDY MATCHING on the caption and never a file name; a backticked token in reader prose.

Sequence-wide: six of eight chapters end on a 'future/proposed extension' paragraph, so the last movement before each exit is a promise about a room that does not exist, and the exits lose their push.

keep.quote: The waiting branch has not disappeared from the graph. It has changed position in the procedure’s pending work.
A queue spreads attention across a frontier; a stack carries it into a branch.
If a claim about the network disappears when the drawing rotates or rearranges, ask whether the claim belonged to the graph or to its presentation.
Search cannot use an option the representation never supplies.
A long and fragile return journey counts as a return journey under this definition.
Redundancy changes meaning when the question changes from cheap connection to surviving a failure.
It leaves us with a question: could some of what was sent earlier be taken back?
Nobody has gained a new connection. We changed which possibility was considered first.

reading.handover_in: ML_Synthesis exits: 'Graph theory will give us another representation of relations. Instead of asking how far points lie from a centre, we will ask which points are connected and what those connections permit.' GT_Foundations opens: 'Can two travellers obey the same connections and encounter the graph in different orders?' The words 'connections' and 'permit' carry straight across (the sequence is titled 'What Connections Permit'), and the machine-learning habit of separating the operation from its interpretation ('A detector's name cannot supply evidence that its flags are useful') is exactly the habit graph theory applies to 'important', 'minimum' and 'maximum'. Registers match: both chapters are about 400 words on the same template. Clean.
reading.handover_out: GT_Matching exits: 'The foundations sequence will question what a formal system can establish. Carry one distinction forward: a procedure meeting its local rule is not automatically a proof of its strongest advertised conclusion.' Euclid_Parallel opens on a plaque counter wrapping (`(current_postulate + 1) % 5`) and reaches 'A rule can feel inevitable long before we have established that it follows', so the thread (rule met is not conclusion proved) lands. The register breaks hard, though: Euclid_Parallel is 1,709 words against Matching's 574, seven numbered sections with headings, five gdscript excerpts, draw tags, a two-voice dialogue ('Fair — and let's say what the array does about it') and a source-editing aside ('In the source, move Line3's offset out to 0.4'). The visitor steps from eight uniform rooms into an annotated source reading. The GT exit line does its job; one concrete foothold (the plaque, the gold) would ease the jump, and the rest is the next sequence's to absorb.

tasks.title: Rejected edges are never marked; the yellow is never cleared
tasks.spec:
[encounter] GT_Spanning_Trees
Quote: “Watch the next edge considered by the display. Before it is accepted or rejected, trace whether its two endpoints are already connected through accepted edges.”
Why: step_kruskal paints the considered edge yellow in place and never restores it; the rejected branch's highlight call is commented out and no red is ever applied, so after the first rejection the reader cannot tell 'the next edge considered' from earlier rejects, and the accepted tree is drawn as a second green line over a yellow one at identical coordinates. The chapter's alternating checks (rejected: trace the cycle; accepted: name the two groups) need three visible states and the hall shows one.
Do: In step_kruskal, before highlighting the next edge restore the previous edge's colour, and colour a rejected edge with the existing rejected_edge_color export (which is declared and never used). Six lines in one function; then the hall shows what the chapter reads: yellow now, green kept, red refused.

tasks.title: Six chapters close on a backlog paragraph
tasks.spec:
[structure] GT_Foundations (also GT_Layout, GT_Pathfinding, GT_Network_Analysis, GT_Spanning_Trees, GT_Flow)
Quote: “A proposed extension could let the group choose one urgent destination and compare the waiting time under each rule.”
Why: The last movement before the exit is, six times in eight, a description of a room that does not exist ('A future extension could expose the search frontier', 'For a proposed extension, let a group spend the cost of one extra edge', 'The next useful experiment would expose a case'). Matching, which replaced its proposed experiment with one the visitor can perform, reads best for exactly this reason.
